\chapter{Farewells}
\label{ch:farewells}
\hlchaptermodality{4}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can end a Tamil conversation politely and choose a farewell that fits the situation.}

Close a conversation the Tamil way out loud: promise to go and come back, answer the same promise, and choose between tomorrow and next-time.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[pō]{\ta{போ} (pō) — \textquotedblleft{}go,\textquotedblright{} and \emph{vā} (come)}

\label{lesson:TA-C04-po}



\begin{quote}
Two of the shortest, oldest verbs in Tamil — and together they make the Tamil goodbye.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ta{போ}} (\emph{pō}, \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{\textbf{vā}} (\textquotedblleft{}to come\textquotedblright{}) are native Dravidian verbs of the deepest layer — single syllables, unchanged for millennia. As bare commands they are already whole words: \emph{pō!} (\textquotedblleft{}go!\textquotedblright{}), \emph{vā!} (\textquotedblleft{}come!\textquotedblright{}). You need both for the next lesson, because Tamil does not say a plain \textquotedblleft{}goodbye\textquotedblright{} — it says \textquotedblleft{}I go, and I \textbf{come back}.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pō\textquotedblright{} (go) and \textquotedblleft{}vā\textquotedblright{} (come)
  \item the commands — \emph{pō!} / \emph{vā!}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do \emph{pō} and \emph{vā} mean, and why will you need them both to say goodbye? (\textquotedblleft{}Go\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{}; the Tamil farewell is \textquotedblleft{}I go and come back,\textquotedblright{} not \textquotedblleft{}I leave.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pōy varugiṟēṉ]{\ta{போய்} \ta{வருகிறேன்} (pōy varugiṟēṉ) — \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TA-C04-poy-varugiren}



\begin{quote}
The everyday Tamil goodbye — and it is, quite literally, a promise to return.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ta{போய்} \ta{வருகிறேன்}} = \textbf{\ta{போய்}} (\emph{pōy}, \textquotedblleft{}having gone\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\ta{வருகிறேன்}} (\emph{varugiṟēṉ}, \textquotedblleft{}I come\textquotedblright{}) — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{having gone, I come},\textquotedblright{} i.e. \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I'll go and come back}.\textquotedblright{} A Tamil speaker never signs off with a bare \textquotedblleft{}I'm leaving\textquotedblright{} — that sounds final, even ill-omened. Instead they promise return. The reply is warm: \emph{\textbf{pōy vā}} (\textquotedblleft{}go and come {[}back{]}\textquotedblright{}).

The same promise, in each language's own words:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}go and come back\textquotedblright{} (goodbye)} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Tamil} & \emph{pōy varugiṟēṉ} \\
Kannada & \emph{hōgi baruttēne} \\
Telugu & \emph{veḷḷi vastānu} \\
Malayalam & \emph{pōyi varāṁ} \\
Bengali (Indo-Aryan) & \emph{āshi} (\textquotedblleft{}I come\textquotedblright{}) \\
Hindi (Indo-Aryan) & \emph{phir milenge} (\textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The whole subcontinent, Dravidian and Indo-Aryan alike, prefers a promise of return to a blunt farewell.

\emph{Varugiṟēṉ} itself is built in three parts: \emph{varu} (\textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{}) + a present-tense marker + \emph{-ēṉ} (\textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}). Chapter 5 makes that stem-tense-person pattern explicit; here it is enough to hear the three pieces.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the \textquotedblleft{}having …d\textquotedblright{} participle}]
\emph{Pōy} is Tamil's way of chaining actions: \textquotedblleft{}having gone, (then) I come.\textquotedblright{} Tamil strings verbs like beads — one in the participle \textquotedblleft{}-y\textquotedblright{} form, the last one fully conjugated. You will see this chaining everywhere.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the goodbye — \emph{pōy varugiṟēṉ}
  \item its literal meaning (\textquotedblleft{}having gone, I come\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}I'll come back\textquotedblright{})
  \item the warm reply — \emph{pōy vā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the Tamil goodbye literally promise, and how do you answer it? (\textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{}; reply \emph{pōy vā}, \textquotedblleft{}go and come {[}back{]}\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nāḷai pārkkalām]{\ta{நாளை} \ta{பார்க்கலாம்} (nāḷai pārkkalām) — \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TA-C04-naalai}



\begin{quote}
A goodbye with a date on it — built on the Tamil word for \textquotedblleft{}day.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ta{நாளை}} (\emph{nāḷai}, \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}) is native Dravidian, from \textbf{\ta{நாள்}} (\emph{nāḷ}, \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}) — the same \emph{nāḷ} in \emph{iṉṟu} / \emph{nāḷ} counting and in \emph{nal-vāḻttukkaḷ} (\textquotedblleft{}good {[}day{]}-wishes\textquotedblright{}). \textbf{\ta{பார்க்கலாம்}} (\emph{pārkkalām}) is \textquotedblleft{}let's see / we may see\textquotedblright{} — \emph{pār} (\textquotedblleft{}to see, to look\textquotedblright{}) plus the ending \emph{-kkalām}, \textquotedblleft{}let's / we may\textquotedblright{} — so the whole phrase is \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{tomorrow, let's see {[}each other{]}},\textquotedblright{} the Tamil \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow.\textquotedblright{} Note the retroflex \textbf{\ta{ள்}} (\emph{ḷ}) — a sound English lacks entirely, made with the tongue-tip curled up and back.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nāḷai pārkkalām\textquotedblright{}
  \item the word for \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} inside \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} (\emph{nāḷ})
  \item the verb \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{} (\emph{pār})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{nāḷai} come from, and what does \emph{pārkkalām} add? (\emph{Nāḷ}, \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}; \textquotedblleft{}let's see\textquotedblright{} — from \emph{pār}, \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{} — so \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow, let's see each other.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mīṇḍum sandippōm]{\ta{மீண்டும்} \ta{சந்திப்போம்} (mīṇḍum sandippōm) — \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TA-C04-mindum-sandippom}



\begin{quote}
A warmer, open-ended goodbye — and a chance to see Tamil's two vocabularies side by side.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ta{மீண்டும்} \ta{சந்திப்போம்}} = \textbf{\ta{மீண்டும்}} (\emph{mīṇḍum}, \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\ta{சந்திப்போம்}} (\emph{sandippōm}, \textquotedblleft{}we will meet\textquotedblright{}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{we'll meet again}.\textquotedblright{} Two vocabularies meet in these two words:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ta{மீண்டும்}} (\emph{mīṇḍum}, \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{}) is \textbf{native Dravidian}, from \emph{mīḷ} (\textquotedblleft{}to return\textquotedblright{}). Say it \emph{mīṇ-ḍum}: the \emph{ṇḍ} in the middle is a retroflex pair, both halves made with the tongue curled back, and it is one gesture rather than two.
  \item \textbf{\ta{சந்தி}} (\emph{sandi}, \textquotedblleft{}to meet, a junction\textquotedblright{}) is a \textbf{Sanskrit} loan — from \emph{sandhi} (\textquotedblleft{}a joining, union\textquotedblright{}), the very word Sanskrit grammar uses for how sounds join at a word-boundary. The ending on it is \emph{-ppōm}, \textquotedblleft{}we will,\textquotedblright{} so \emph{sandippōm} is \textquotedblleft{}we will meet.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

So even a goodbye shows Tamil's balance: an ancient Dravidian core (\emph{mīṇḍum}) beside a Sanskrit borrowing (\emph{sandi}) — the recurring thread of this whole track.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mīṇḍum sandippōm\textquotedblright{}
  \item which word is native Dravidian and which is Sanskrit (\emph{mīṇḍum} / \emph{sandi})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the phrase mean, and which of its two words is the Sanskrit loan? (\textquotedblleft{}We'll meet again\textquotedblright{}; \emph{sandi} \textquotedblleft{}to meet\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{sandhi} — while \emph{mīṇḍum} \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{} is native Dravidian.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tamiḻ eḻuttu]{Tamil's curves — the writing surface leaves a trace}

\label{lesson:TA-W01-curves-va-ka}



\begin{quote}
Before the first letter, look at a line of Tamil and notice what isn't there:

\begin{quote}
\ta{வணக்கம்}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Nothing joins the letters together}, and there are far fewer corners than in Devanagari — no hanging head-line, and a great deal of curve. (Straight strokes do exist: most of these letters have a flat bar across the top.) The roundness has a usual explanation, and it is the best story in this chapter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: The script is the shape of its writing surface}
Tamil was written for centuries on \textbf{palm leaves}, scratched with a metal stylus and then rubbed with soot to make the scratches show.

A palm leaf has a \textbf{grain}, like wood. Draw a long straight line along that grain and the stylus can \textbf{split the leaf}. The usual account is that scribes bent their strokes in response: a curve crosses the fibres at an angle instead of running with them.

Treat that as \textbf{the standard explanation rather than a settled fact.} The earliest Tamil writing — Tamil-Brahmi, cut into stone and pottery — is noticeably \emph{angular}; the rounding came later, through the Vaṭṭeḻuttu (\textquotedblleft{}round script\textquotedblright{}) stage. And Devanagari was written on the same leaves without going round. So the leaf is one pressure among several, not a complete answer.

It is still worth carrying, because it makes the right general point: \textbf{the tool leaves fingerprints on the letters.} Latin's straight strokes suit a wax tablet and a chisel; Tamil's curves suit a stylus and a leaf.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} a curve crossing the imagined grain of a palm leaf
  \item \emph{Contrast:} angular Tamil-Brahmi · later rounded Vaṭṭeḻuttu
  \item \emph{Say it:} the usual reason for the curves — \textquotedblleft{}a straight line can \textbf{split the leaf}\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why is Tamil round? (The \textbf{usual} explanation: it was incised on \textbf{palm leaves}, where a straight stroke along the grain can \textbf{split} them — though early Tamil-Brahmi was angular, so it is not the whole story.) What broader point does the account teach? (\textbf{Tools and surfaces leave fingerprints on scripts.}) Next: the chapter's own recap of the farewells.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 4 — The farewells}

\label{lesson:TA-C04-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Three ways to part — none of them a blunt \textquotedblleft{}goodbye.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn — the farewells}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the everyday goodbye — \emph{pōy varugiṟēṉ} (\textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{})
  \item the warm reply — \emph{pōy vā} (\textquotedblleft{}go and come back\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{} — \emph{nāḷai pārkkalām}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{} — \emph{mīṇḍum sandippōm}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn — the atoms}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the two oldest verbs (\emph{pō} go, \emph{vā} come)
  \item \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} hidden in \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} (\emph{nāḷ})
  \item which farewell-word is a Sanskrit loan (\emph{sandi} $\leftarrow$ \emph{sandhi})
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — roots you now carry}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pōy varugiṟēṉ} — \textquotedblleft{}having gone, I come\textquotedblright{}; the Dravidian promise-of-return goodbye
  \item \emph{nāḷai} $\leftarrow$ \emph{nāḷ} \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}; \emph{pār} \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{mīṇḍum} (native \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{sandi} (Sanskrit \textquotedblleft{}to meet\textquotedblright{}) — the two vocabularies
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does Tamil never say a plain \textquotedblleft{}I'm leaving,\textquotedblright{} and what does its everyday goodbye promise instead? (It sounds final/ill-omened; \emph{pōy varugiṟēṉ} promises \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
